subject: maths
title: Real-life maths missions
seo_title: Real-life maths problems for ages 9 to 14: missions with money, time and more
description: Real-life maths word problems as story missions: plan a party on a budget, bake for the school fair, plan a train trip, design a garden, run sports day and save up for a bike. Multi-step problems with hints, for ages 9 to 14.
intro: Maths isn't just for school. Each mission is a story where you use Maths to make real decisions: money, time, recipes, space and data. Read carefully, and use the hints if you get stuck.

units.title: Mission 1: Party planner
units.blurb: Plan a birthday party for 12 friends with a £60 budget.

learn.p: You are planning a party for **12 guests** (you included). You have a budget of **£60**. Pizzas cost £6.50 each and one pizza feeds 3 people. Party bags cost £1.75 each. Balloons come in packs of 10 for £2.40.
Read each question twice. Underline the numbers you need. Write down each step, and check your answer makes sense: you can't buy half a pizza!

questions.q: One pizza feeds 3 people. How many pizzas do you need for 12 people?
questions.hint: How many groups of 3 are there in 12?

questions.q: Pizzas cost £6.50 each. How many pounds do 4 pizzas cost?
Party bags cost £1.75 each. How many pounds do 12 party bags cost?
You want 25 balloons. Balloons come in packs of 10. How many packs must you buy?
questions.hint: 2 packs give 20 balloons. Is that enough?
questions.explain: 2 packs = 20 balloons, not enough. You need 3 packs (30 balloons).

questions.q: Pizzas £26, party bags £21 and 3 packs of balloons at £2.40 each. What is the total, in pounds?
Your budget is £60. How much money is left, in pounds?
With the money left, can you buy a £4.99 cake?

units.title: Mission 2: Bake for the school fair
units.blurb: Scale a recipe up and work out your profit.

learn.p: This recipe makes **12 cookies**: 200 g flour, 100 g butter, 80 g sugar, 1 egg. You need **36 cookies** for the school fair, and you'll sell them for 40p each.
If you need 3 times as many cookies, you need 3 times as much of every ingredient. That's using a **ratio**: the amounts stay in proportion.

questions.q: How many times bigger is 36 cookies than 12 cookies?
questions.explain: 36 ÷ 12 = 3. You need to make the recipe 3 times bigger.

questions.q: How many grams of flour do you need for 36 cookies?
How many grams of sugar do you need for 36 cookies?
Butter comes in 250 g blocks. How many blocks do you need for 300 g?
questions.explain: 1 block = 250 g, not enough. 2 blocks = 500 g. You need 2 blocks.

questions.q: You sell all 36 cookies at 40p each. How many pounds do you take?
The ingredients cost £5.90. How much profit do you make, in pounds?
One batch of 12 takes 15 minutes in the oven, and only one batch fits at a time. How many minutes for all 36?

units.title: Mission 3: The big train trip
units.blurb: Read a timetable and plan a day out.

learn.p: Your family is going to the seaside by train. Trains leave town at **08:45, 09:20 and 10:15**. The journey takes **1 hour 35 minutes**. Adult tickets cost £18.50 and child tickets are half price.
Timetables use the 24-hour clock. To add a time, add the hours first, then the minutes, and remember there are 60 minutes in an hour.

questions.q: You take the 09:20 train. When do you arrive?
You must arrive by 11:00. Which is the latest train you can catch?
questions.explain: The 10:15 arrives at 11:50, too late. The 09:20 arrives at 10:55, just in time.

questions.q: A child ticket is half of £18.50. How much is it, in pounds?
Tickets for 2 adults and 2 children. What is the total, in pounds?
You leave the beach at 16:10 and the train home arrives at 17:45. How many minutes is that?
The train travels 120 km in 1 hour 30 minutes. How many km is that per hour?
questions.hint: In 30 minutes it goes a third of the way. So in 1 hour…
questions.explain: 1 hour 30 minutes is 3 lots of 30 minutes. 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km every 30 minutes, so 80 km per hour.

units.title: Mission 4: Design a garden
units.blurb: Fences, grass and flower beds: perimeter and area.

learn.p: Your school has a rectangle of land **12 m long and 8 m wide** for a new garden. You need a fence round the outside, grass seed for the lawn, and a square flower bed **3 m by 3 m**.
**Perimeter** is the distance round the edge (metres). **Area** is the space inside (square metres, m²). Area of a rectangle = length × width.

questions.q: How many metres of fence go all the way round the garden?
There is a 2 m wide gate in the fence. How many metres of fence do you buy?
What is the area of the whole garden?
What is the area of the square flower bed?
The rest of the garden is grass. What is the area of the grass?
questions.hint: Whole garden minus the flower bed.

questions.q: One box of grass seed covers 30 m². How many boxes do you need for 87 m²?
questions.hint: 2 boxes cover 60 m². Is that enough?
questions.explain: 2 boxes cover 60 m², not enough. 3 boxes cover 90 m². You need 3 boxes.

units.title: Mission 5: Sports day data
units.blurb: Use averages to report on the long jump.

learn.p: You are the sports day reporter. Five jumps in the long jump were: **2.1 m, 2.5 m, 1.8 m, 2.5 m and 2.6 m**. You need to work out some numbers for the school newsletter.

The **mean** is the total divided by how many there are. The **median** is the middle value when they are in order. The **mode** is the most common value. The **range** is the biggest minus the smallest.

questions.q: What is the longest jump, in metres?
What is the range of the jumps, in metres?
What is the mode?
questions.hint: Which jump length appears more than once?
questions.explain: 2.5 m appears twice, so the mode is 2.5 m.

questions.q: Put the jumps in order. What is the median?
questions.explain: In order: 1.8, 2.1, 2.5, 2.5, 2.6. The middle one is 2.5 m.

questions.q: What is the total of all five jumps, in metres?
What is the mean jump, in metres?

units.title: Mission 6: Saving up for a bike
units.blurb: Percentages, discounts and a savings plan.

learn.p: You want a bike that costs **£180**. You already have **£45**. You get **£7.50 pocket money a week**. The shop has a sale coming soon.
Per cent means “out of 100”. 10% is {1/10}, so 10% of £180 is £18. 25% is {1/4} and 50% is {1/2}.

questions.q: How much more money do you need, in pounds?
You save all your £7.50 a week. How many pounds do you save in 4 weeks?
How many weeks does it take to save £135 at £7.50 a week?
questions.hint: £30 every 4 weeks. How many lots of £30 make £135? You'll need a bit more than 4 lots.

questions.q: The sale takes 20% off the £180 price. How much is 20% of £180, in pounds?
What is the sale price of the bike, in pounds?
With the sale price, how much more do you need after your £45, in pounds?
How many weeks of saving £7.50 does that take? (Round up to whole weeks.)
questions.explain: 13 weeks = £97.50, just short. 14 weeks = £105, enough. So 14 weeks: 4 weeks sooner than without the sale.
